Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-dream.md

# f-dream

Look back over past jobs: merge repeated lessons and spot mistakes that keep happening.

Command: `/f-dream`

Stage: Merge, close and Logbook · The Logbook
Source: `skills/f-dream/SKILL.md`

## On site

The Logbook: now and then. It shows what it would change first, and only applies it with your permission. Every change can be undone, and it never removes a card marked critical.

## Say it

- "reflect across the jobs"
- "are we repeating mistakes"
- "clean up contradictions in the logbook"

## When to use it

Now and then, to tidy the Logbook: merge repeats and spot patterns.

## Not for

Reconciles content: not for promoting knowledge upward (f-distill), nor for rotating by count (f-archive).

## It's working if

- By default it reads the last ten completed jobs and returns a numbered proposal, writing nothing.
- Each proposed change cites its evidence, its target cards, the relationship changes, a confidence and a rollback.
- The proposal holds at most 10 changes and never retires a CRITICAL card on its own.
- The output gives the proposal ID, the corpus size, merges, supersessions, new patterns and anything skipped or flagged.
- When applied, each retired card is copied and the copy checked before the live copy is removed, and an applied manifest can reverse every change.
- It staged, committed and pushed nothing.

## Common questions

### Does a plain run change anything?

No. The default is a dry run. It suggests a path for the proposal, but saves it only with `--save-proposal` and your explicit write authority.

### How do I apply a proposal?

Run `--apply --proposal <id>` with the saved proposal's id. It applies only the accepted items, and there is no "most recent" default.

### What does it treat as a duplicate or a contradiction?

It checks every candidate against its source. The same lesson in different contexts is not a duplicate, and advice that depends on context is not a contradiction.

### Can I choose which jobs it reads?

Yes: `--since` and `--jobs` bound the set.

### When does it stop partway?

On an unclear card identity, missing provenance, a copy that fails its check, or links that don't add up.

### How is it different from `/f-archive`?

`/f-archive` rotates cards out by count and judges nothing. This reads the content and reconciles it.


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-greploop.md

# f-greploop

Run an open pull request through Greptile's review, up to three rounds.

Command: `/f-greploop`

Stage: Merge, close and Logbook · PR and merge · step 9 of 11 in the order of works (Review the PR)
Source: `skills/f-greploop/SKILL.md`

## On site

After you open the pull request and say "greploop", before you say "merge". Then the pull request's description is checked, on every job. Each finding is checked, the builder makes the fixes, the tests run again every round, and the fixes are pushed with your permission.

## Say it

- "merge"
- "greploop"

## When to use it

After the pull request is open, when you say "greploop".

## Not for

The lens inspection (f-inspect) or the independent inspection (xreview); never merges.

## It's working if

- It checks the PR's head matches the job's final head before asking for a review.
- It asks with the comment `@greptileai review` exactly, once per round, and waits with the bundled `greptile-wait.mjs`, not a hand-rolled loop.
- Every Greptile finding gets a recorded disposition, even on a 5/5 score.
- Accepted findings go to the builder as test-first repair work orders; the foreman fixes nothing itself.
- Tests, base-vs-head and the acceptance ledger are green at the new head before any push, and pushes are never forced.
- It stops after round 3 at the latest and hands over with each round's score, the open findings and the commits added.
- The PR body is checked against the final diff before it tells you the PR is ready, and it never merges.

## Common questions

### What does "greploop" let it do?

For this PR only and at most three rounds: post the review request and push reviewed repair commits to the PR's branch. Nothing else: no merge, no other branch, no other comment. A fourth round needs your word again. Inside an autonomous run you started for this job, the goal's own words grant this instead.

### Does it resolve Greptile's threads?

No. Threads stay as they are; each round's record says which findings are fixed and by which commit. A finding is never dismissed as noise without saying so.

### Why re-run the tests if Greptile gives 5/5?

Greptile reads the code but runs nothing. A fix made to please it can still break a test or undo a requirement, so every round that changes code re-runs the mechanical checks before the push.

### What if Greptile never answers?

The waiter gives up after 10 minutes and the skill halts and tells you. A failed read is reported as an error, and a score is never invented.

### What if a finding needs a locked decision changed?

That is a halt. It shows you the conflict instead of changing a locked decision, the constitution or a requirement to satisfy Greptile.

### Does it merge when it reaches 5/5?

No. It ends with "5/5, ready for your merge" or "stopped after round N: your call". The merge stays a separate step: your word, or covered by an autonomous run you started for this job.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-inspect
- Uses: adjudicate


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-inspect.md

# f-inspect

Have specialist reviewers check the finished job's changes and report only problems.

Command: `/f-inspect` (old name `/f-lens`)

Stage: Inspect · The end game · step 7 of 11 in the order of works (Inspect)
Source: `skills/f-inspect/SKILL.md`

## On site

Near the end of a job, the first of two reviews: the foreman runs it once the build is finished, before any pull request. Small, low-risk jobs skip it. It reviews only this job's changes, makes no fixes and gives no verdict, just findings. The record goes in templates/LENS-INSPECTION.md.

## Say it

- "run the lens inspection"

## When to use it

When a job's build is finished and its tests pass, before the pull request is opened.

## Not for

The independent inspection (pack-review → xreview → adjudicate), not a review of an open PR (f-greploop).

## It's working if

- It stops and says so when `foreman/jobs/` holds no job file for the slug, instead of reviewing anyway.
- It stops and reports a wrong HEAD or an unexpected dirty file, and never checks out, stashes or resets anything.
- It lists which lenses ran and which were skipped, each with a reason, and `lens-simplify` ran last as report-only.
- Every finding carries severity, confidence, file:line, the scenario, why it matters and a concrete remedy.
- Each lens is asked whether, where a test proves something is absent (no raw amount, no secret), another test pins the exact value shown.
- A lens that halted, errored or returned `BLOCK` is reported as such, not as a clean lens with zero findings.
- The findings are written to `<day folder>/JOB-<N>-LENS-INSPECTION.md`.
- It gave no SHIP or BLOCK verdict, fixed nothing, and made no commit, push or PR.

## How it pins the scope

These are the checks it runs before any lens reads the work, shown exactly as the skill lists them.

```
WT="<worktree>"; BASE="<base sha>"; HEAD_SHA="<final head sha>"
git -C "$WT" rev-parse HEAD                      # must equal $HEAD_SHA: stop if not
git -C "$WT" status --short                      # only the profile's dirty-file allowlist
git -C "$WT" diff --name-status "$BASE..$HEAD_SHA"   # the manifest the lenses review
git -C "$WT" diff "$BASE..$HEAD_SHA" > "<day folder>/lens/<ticket>.diff"
```

## Common questions

### Why is there no PR yet?

This inspection runs after gate 2 and before the PR is prepared. The PR comes only after both inspections, the final re-run and the acceptance ledger.

### Does every job get it?

No. QUICK jobs skip it, and the record says `lens inspection: SKIP (QUICK)`. STANDARD and FULL jobs get it.

### Who fixes what it finds?

Not this skill. The findings go to adjudication, where each is reproduced against the code and accepted, rejected or partly accepted. Accepted findings become the builder's test-first repair work orders.

### Why does each lens start fresh?

Each triggered lens runs as a new subagent with no context from the job, so it reads the work cold. It is briefed with the range, the diff, the ticket's goal and constraints, and the settled decisions it must not relitigate.

### How is it different from the independent inspection?

This is the first of a job's two inspections, run by the foreman in its own session. The independent inspection (`/pack-review`, `/xreview`, `/adjudicate`) comes after, with a reviewer in another session.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/f-lens` still works.

## Connections

- Leads to: f-greploop, pack-review
- Uses: lens-code, lens-comments, lens-errors, lens-instructions, lens-migrations, lens-simplify, lens-tests, lens-types


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-night-shift.md

# f-night-shift

Run several jobs one after another without you: a shift boss opens a fresh foreman for each.

Command: `/f-night-shift`

Stage: Kit · Several jobs in a row
Source: `skills/f-night-shift/SKILL.md`

## On site

When you type /goal night shift with a list of jobs, or a number of jobs to pick: usually before you sleep. Each job is its own autonomous run; the boss only starts it and checks the repo. Any stop ends the shift, and so does a completed topping out (the next head is yours to pick); the morning summary is one file.

## Say it

- "/goal night shift: jobs 13, 17, until done or stopped"
- "/goal night shift: 2 jobs, auto-pick, until done or stopped"

## When to use it

Before you sleep, when the next jobs are on the board and you want them built one after another without you.

## Not for

One job (that is "/goal autonomous run: <opener>"), and never inside a job's own foreman session.

## It's working if

- It copies your exact /goal words into the shift record before doing anything else.
- It refuses to start unless main matches the remote, the last job's end game is finished and no job worktree is open.
- It never plans, builds, reviews or merges: each job runs in its own fresh foreman session.
- It decides a job is done from the repo (merged, end game clear, next opener written), never from what the chat says.
- The first stop ends the whole shift, with the foreman's stop line quoted in the shift record.
- In planned mode it stops if a job's end game picks a job that is not next on your list.

## Common questions

### How do I start one?

In a fresh session, type `/goal night shift: jobs 13, 14` to run a list you chose, or `/goal night shift: 2 jobs, auto-pick` to let each job's end game pick the next. Add `, spend up to 5 USD` to allow paid checks, one cap for the whole shift. Only your own typed line starts a shift.

### What does the shift boss do?

It opens a fresh foreman for each job, types that job's autonomous run, and checks the repo until the job is merged and closed. Then it starts the next. It never answers a job's questions or types into its session after the start line.

### What happens when a job stops?

The shift ends. The boss writes the reason into the shift record, quoting the foreman's own stop line, and tells you in one short reply. Nothing after the stop runs.

### What if the builder hits its usage limit?

The job pauses, it doesn't stop: the foreman waits for the limit to reset and carries on, and the shift waits with it. It never switches to a paid seat or another builder. A reset more than six hours away, or unknown, stops the job. If the foreman's own session hits its limit, the boss sends it one fixed line after the reset and it carries on.

### How is it different from one autonomous run?

`/goal autonomous run: <opener>` runs one job without you. A night shift runs several in a row, each one its own autonomous run in a fresh session.

### What does it need from my repo?

The foreman launch command in your repo profile (for example `claude`, with the flags you use), the first job's opener in `foreman/handovers/`, and Orca to open each foreman in its own tab. If the launch command is missing, it stops and asks rather than guessing.

### How long can a shift run?

Until the list is done, a job stops, a board tops out, the spend cap is reached, or a single job runs past 16 hours.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-signoff


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-plancheck.md

# f-plancheck

Have AI models from other companies read the plan fresh and point out problems.

Command: `/f-plancheck` (old name `/plan-read`)

Stage: Plan · Before a job · step 3 of 11 in the order of works (Check the plan)
Source: `skills/f-plancheck/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before a job, step 3, between f-blueprint and f-schedule: the plan has to pass this check before it's split into jobs. One to five AI models from other companies read the plan side by side, all with the same checklist, and their findings are combined, never voted on.

## When to use it

After a plan is written and before it's split into jobs; also on a job's own plan before its second work order.

## It's working if

- Before picking seats, it prints who wrote the plan and which model family is excluded, so no seat comes from the author's own family.
- On an attended run, it opens a one-shot picker in your browser and posts the picker's link in chat; nothing is dispatched until you have picked 1 to 5 seats.
- Each seat gets the ticket's own words and checks every decision against them as well as against the code.
- It reports the findings of the mechanical checks (paths, `file:line` citations, CLI flags, measurements, the Done-when block) as findings, without fixing them.
- It writes `findings.md` in a fresh scratch folder: one block per defect, each with where, which seats raised it, the evidence, and an empty Disposition line.
- Findings that change what is built sit in their own section, marked DO NOT ACT and left for your decision, with no suggested fix, and the report shows each of them to you in full.
- The plan is untouched apart from one `gate: plancheck` line, which a plan in or headed for `foreman/blueprints/ready/` always gets.
- It staged, committed and pushed nothing.

## Common questions

### Why can't the model that wrote the plan check it?

That would be self-review. Seats come only from model families other than the plan's author and the session host; the picker greys those out and its server refuses them.

### Do the seats vote?

No. Identical defects at the same place are merged and credited to every seat that raised it. A finding from one seat reaches you exactly as one from every seat, and none is averaged away.

### Will it fix the plan for me?

No. It reports defects and evidence, and carries a seat's suggested fix only as a suggestion. Applying findings is a separate step, done by the plan's author after you have seen them.

### When does it say the plan needs rewriting?

When three or more verified critical findings land, or any finding goes against the plan's premise. It then says to rewrite from the intent, rather than listing patches.

### Does it cost money?

The codex, Claude and Grok CLI seats run on subscriptions. OpenRouter seats are pay-per-token and need `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. An unattended run uses only the subscription seats.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/plan-read` still works, and `/cv` is an alias. Older plans may carry `gate: plan-read`, the same gate under its old name.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-blueprint
- Leads to: f-schedule
- Uses: plan-validator
- Used by: f-shift


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-schedule.md

# f-schedule

Split a big plan into jobs, in order, and draw the project board.

Command: `/f-schedule` (old name `/f-decompose`)

Stage: Plan · Before a job · step 4 of 11 in the order of works (Cut into tickets)
Source: `skills/f-schedule/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before a job, step 4: it won't start on a plan that hasn't passed the plan check, and it waits for your go before writing anything. Anything that needs research or your decision becomes its own job, every requirement belongs to a job, and the ticket wording is copied exactly. It writes the project's folder and its board.

## Say it

- "break this plan into tickets"
- "decompose this into jobs"
- "turn this plan into a project"

## When to use it

When a plan has passed the plan check and is ready to be split into jobs.

## Not for

Writing the plan (f-blueprint), not for planning one ticket's job (the foreman's scoping + PLAN.md), not for board updates after that (f-board).

## It's working if

- On a plan without the `gate: plancheck` line, it stops and tells you to run `/f-plancheck` first. A findings row with a blank fate stops it too.
- Before writing anything, it shows you the head, the job table, the decision jobs, any unmapped verification points or tasks, any disagreements, and the job it recommends first.
- It writes nothing until you say "go" for the project.
- Research and owner decisions are their own jobs, never hidden inside another: a question that ends in your answer is a decision job; research that produces a file is a build job and goes through a PR.
- Every verification point is carried by at least one job, and every plan task maps to a job or to "not carried, on purpose" with its reason.
- `foreman/projects/<slug>/` holds `PROJECT.md`, one ticket file per job with the acceptance quoted, and a `BOARD.json` that `render_board.py` validated and rendered.
- It committed nothing, and never deleted or rewrote the source plan.

## The two ways to run it

The two forms of the command, exactly as the skill lists them.

```
/f-schedule <path to BLUEPRINT>            # propose the cut, then write on go
/f-schedule --split <project-slug> <job-id>  # split one job that scoping found too big
```

## Common questions

### How big is one job?

One ticket, one PR, one module area, sized for roughly 8 to 9 work orders. A plan bigger than that becomes a project.

### Does it publish the board page straight away?

No. Publishing the board page and adding a note to the source plan are each a separate word from you, after the project is written.

### What if scoping later finds a job is too big?

Run `/f-schedule --split <project-slug> <job-id>`. The children replace the job, dependents are rewired, and every verification point is still carried. A merged or decision job can't be split.

### We use a ticket tracker. Will it create tickets there?

No. It maps each job to an existing key where one fits and never mints a new one. Where the tracker and the plan disagree, the difference goes on your list.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/f-decompose` still works.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-plancheck
- Uses: simplicity-critic, f-board


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-search.md

# f-search

Find Logbook cards about a topic.

Command: `/f-search`

Stage: Merge, close and Logbook · The Logbook
Source: `skills/f-search/SKILL.md`

## On site

The Logbook: any time. f-shift uses it to load the lessons that apply to a job. Searches current cards only; older ones are in f-archive-search.

## When to use it

When you want to know what past jobs learned about a topic.

## It's working if

- It returns at most 10 cards, each with its id, type, cluster, tags, a short overview and its path.
- Every hit is a live card under `foreman/logbook/entries/`, never one from `foreman/logbook/archived/`.
- The card templates never show up as hits, even in an empty Logbook.
- When nothing matches, it says so and points you to `/f-archive-search`, with no made-up list of cards.
- There are no ranking scores or stats tables in the output.

## Common questions

### How do I write a query?

Mix plain keywords, `#tag`, `@cluster` and `type:insight`, `type:method` or `type:build`. The filters combine with AND; a card matches the keywords if it contains any of them, ignoring case.

### Where do the cluster names come from?

From your own cards. The `## Clusters` section of `logbook_index.md` lists the ones in use. If a cluster search finds suspiciously few cards, it retries the same word as a keyword before saying they don't exist.

### Why can't it find a lesson I know we learned?

It reads live cards only. If the card was rotated out by `/f-archive`, search for it with `/f-archive-search`.

### Does it look anywhere besides the Logbook files?

No. It is told to read only the live Logbook files, even if the repo has its own card database or search service.

## Connections

- Leads to: f-archive-search
- Used by: f-shift


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-setup.md

# f-setup

Install the method into a repo or upgrade it, write the repo profile, and prove the install.

Command: `/f-setup`

Stage: Kit · Setting up
Source: `skills/f-setup/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before the first job, once per repo, and again for each upgrade (never while a job is open). The first time, the skill isn't in the repo yet: tell the session to read the package's skills/f-setup/SKILL.md and follow it. It reads the repo for the gates, remotes and keys before asking you anything, never overwrites a file the repo already has, and never commits.

## Say it

- "set up Topping Out here"
- "install the method"
- "upgrade Topping Out"

## When to use it

When a repo should start running the method, or a newer package should go over an existing install.

## It's working if

- It copies only what's missing and never overwrites a file the repo already has; only an upgrade replaces a file, and only one unchanged since the last install.
- The repo profile is written from what the repo actually has, and you're asked only what it couldn't find, in one batch.
- Every profile row is filled; a row nothing can answer yet says `not recorded` and why.
- The names files exist, are git-ignored and never empty, and the names check proves itself on this machine.
- The test adapter is proved on two fixtures: only the test failing at head alone is reported.
- It never stages, commits or pushes: it ends with the list of files for your commit.
- It ends with one line: `F-SETUP: READY <profile path>` or `F-SETUP: HALTED <reason>`.

## Common questions

### How do I run it the first time?

In the repo that will hold your records, start a session and say `Read <path to the package>/skills/f-setup/SKILL.md and follow it`. The install copies the skill too, so every later run is just `/f-setup`.

### How do I update later?

Run `/f-setup` again. With a receipt in the repo it upgrades: files you didn't adapt are replaced, files you did are listed for a merge by hand. It refuses while a job is open or an end game is owed.

### What does it ask me?

Only what the repo can't answer: typically the product name, ticket mode, board publish mode, the budgets and the builders' names. Each question offers the answer it found as the default.

### What is the first question?

Whether the product is an AI agent built on LangChain, LangGraph or Deep Agents. A yes adds the Deep Agents add-on: `/deep`, a reference checked against the real `deepagents` code, and LangChain's docs server. A no skips it, and nothing else changes.

### Does it touch my secrets?

It reads the names of keys in `.env` files, never their values, and never prints a value.

### How do I remove Topping Out?

The receipt, `foreman/INSTALL-RECEIPT.txt`, lists every file the package installed. Delete those you haven't adapted, then the receipt. Your records stay yours.

## Connections

- Uses: f-board, f-signoff


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-shift.md

# f-shift

Start a session as the foreman: read the role, the rules and the playbook first.

Command: `/f-shift`

Stage: Run a job · Starting and running a job · step 5 of 11 in the order of works (Start the shift)
Source: `skills/f-shift/SKILL.md`

## On site

Job start: the first command of every new session. It loads the lessons from past jobs that apply to this one. It reads the method, the rules, the playbook and the builder's notes, checks the job's facts for itself, then looks over the repo before any work starts.

## Say it

- "you are the foreman"
- "be the foreman"
- "set up as foreman"

## When to use it

At the start of every foreman session, before looking at any ticket.

## Not for

The builder's side (the builder gets work orders, never this skill), not for cutting a plan into tickets (f-schedule), not for updating the board (f-board).

## It's working if

- If the last job's close-out isn't finished, it stops at the end-game lock and names the missing steps.
- It reads the method files in full: `README.md`, `RULES.md` with its "Foreman rules" section, `METHOD.md`, `OVERRIDES.md`, `Foreman-Playbook.md` and `BUILDER-PROFILES.md`, then the job's own handover and ticket.
- Its first reply confirms the job's facts: the ticket and project, the builder, form A or B, the delivery, the repos and day folder, the gates, and what needs your word this job (and, if you started an autonomous run, which of those acts its goal covers).
- Anything unclear is measured or listed as an owed question, not assumed.
- It lists the Logbook cards in force for the job's area, CRITICAL and HIGH first.
- It runs the site walk, then stops and waits for your "go".
- Every reply ends with the 5-line status block.

## Common questions

### When do I run it?

At the start of every job, before scoping a ticket. It is what makes the session the foreman.

### Does the builder use it?

No. The builder only gets work orders, never this skill.

### What if this is the first Topping Out job in the repo?

There is no shift handover yet. It reads the repo profile instead, measures every fact itself, and marks the handover rows "not applicable: first job".

### Why does it read everything in full instead of summarising?

The foreman makes every design decision and writes every work order, and the builder's discipline can't rescue a wrong decision. Loading the role line by line keeps any of it from being skimmed.

### What if there are a lot of Logbook cards?

More than 250 live cards means it runs `/f-archive` first.

## Connections

- Uses: f-archive, f-board, f-search, f-plancheck


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-signoff.md

# f-signoff

Close a merged job: check every requirement passed, save the lessons, file the job away.

Command: `/f-signoff` (old name `/f-close`)

Stage: Merge, close and Logbook · Close · step 11 of 11 in the order of works (Close)
Source: `skills/f-signoff/SKILL.md`

## On site

After the merge: closes the job only when every requirement has passed, with nothing put off for later. Then come the dev report, the choice of the next job, the board update and the handover, in that order. At the board's head it tops the project out instead: a topping out report, the frozen board, and candidate next heads for you to pick from.

## Say it

- "close this job"
- "we're done, wrap it up"

## When to use it

Right after a job's pull request is merged and the merge is confirmed.

## Not for

Committing or pushing (the owner's word).

## It's working if

- On a build job that isn't merged, it refuses and points to the PR instead.
- Every row of the acceptance ledger is PASS. A row that isn't stops the close: there is no "close anyway".
- It shows a drift audit, planned but not built against built but not planned. An empty table is the normal result.
- The job file has moved to `foreman/completed-jobs/<YYYY-MM>/` and is gone from `foreman/jobs/`.
- The last line reads `F-SIGNOFF: SIGNED OFF <archive path>`, followed by the end-game checklist.
- It staged, committed and pushed nothing, and the blueprint is untouched.

## How every close ends

The close report ends with this checklist, exactly as the skill prints it, so the next steps are read, not remembered.

```
END-GAME OWED for job <NN> (foreman/ENDGAME-PENDING.md), in this order:
1. dev report            -> endgame.mjs tick dev-report --file <path>
2. next-ticket decision  -> endgame.mjs tick next-ticket-decision --file <path>
   then the owner confirms (or, under a /goal, the foreman records the goal): the file's
   "Owner confirmed:" line must be filled before step 2b
2b. ground investigation -> endgame.mjs tick ground-investigation --file <day folder>/JOB-<next>-GROUND-INVESTIGATION.md
   (METHOD.md §10 step 7b: four read-only research agents, one per angle, plus the profile's framework check;
   the handover and the opener point to it)
3. board close event     -> endgame.mjs tick board --file <project>/BOARD.json   (every project has one; none yet: render_board.py … init)
4. shift handover + opener -> endgame.mjs tick handover --file <handover> --opener foreman/handovers/OPENER-JOB-<next>.txt, then endgame.mjs clear
   (then give the owner the opener's path and **three ways to start the next job, each ready to paste**:
    normal: paste the opener's text into a fresh session;
    autonomous run: /goal autonomous run: <absolute opener path>, until done or stopped;
    night shift: /goal night shift: jobs <next board id>, <the one after, from the board>, until done or stopped;
    adding ", spend up to <n> USD (read, or a ceiling under it)" to the last two when the next job has a paid seat or a live-key walkthrough, and
    listing the questions its survey will answer itself under a goal (its ground investigation's starred picks))
5. records push         -> names check over everything staged (names-check.mjs --staged, METHOD.md §10 step 9; a hit is rewritten first), merge <remote>/<main> into
                           the records branch (never a rebase), check only records differ, push; then check CI on main
                           (gh run list -R <target repo> -b <main> -L 1): red is reported, never called green

TOPPING OUT (the decision says "Topping out: yes": every job merged or resolved, or the owner's words; METHOD.md §11b):
    first the board events (not locked): an in-progress build job: close <job> --pr ... --merge <M> [--no-next --reason "topping out"];
    a decision job: decided <job> --note "<the owner's decision>"; already merged or resolved: nothing; then
    render_board.py <project>/BOARD.json topout --report <day folder>/TOPPING-OUT-REPORT.md [--quote "<the owner's words>"]
2b. topping out report  -> write it from the topped-out board's check output, then
                           endgame.mjs tick ground-investigation --file <day folder>/TOPPING-OUT-REPORT.md
3.  board               -> endgame.mjs tick board --file <project>/BOARD.json   (must be topped out)
4.  next heads          -> endgame.mjs tick handover --file <day folder>/NEXT-HEADS.md (no opener), then endgame.mjs clear
    (then tell the owner the project topped out, and give the candidate heads, the evidence's pick first, with how each starts)
```

## Common questions

### Can I close a job that isn't quite finished?

No. Finish it, or record your own scope decision in the acceptance ledger. A job that can't finish is halted on the board, not closed.

### What if the close is interrupted halfway?

Each stage is recorded in the job file with the hash of what it wrote. A retry resumes from the first unfinished stage and never repeats a completed write. If a file doesn't match its recorded hash, it stops and reports every stage's state.

### Does it commit or push?

No. File moves are plain moves; you commit them when you choose.

### Why doesn't it retire the blueprint?

A job builds one ticket of a project. The blueprint is archived only after its board tops out, and only on your word. If you top out with jobs carried over, the carried work lives on in the topping out report.

### What comes after it?

The dev report, then the next-ticket decision, which you confirm. Then the board's close event, and the shift handover with the next session's opener beside it (`foreman/handovers/OPENER-JOB-<N>.txt`, which you get to paste). Nothing new starts until those are done; then the records are pushed.

### What happens at the board's head?

The last job closes with no next job, the board tops out (`topout`), and in place of the handover you get a topping out report and three to five candidate next heads. There is no opener: you pick the next head when you're ready.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/f-close` still works.

## Connections

- Leads to: f-board, f-night-shift
- Uses: spec-validator-fixer
- Used by: f-setup

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-sketch.md

# f-sketch

Write down a rough idea and its open questions, before anything is decided.

Command: `/f-sketch` (old name `/f-idea`)

Stage: Plan · Before a job · step 1 of 11 in the order of works (Shape the idea)
Source: `skills/f-sketch/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before a job, the very first step: when an idea is worth keeping but not ready to decide. A notes file, not a plan: what's agreed so far, the open questions and the options turned down. When it's ready it moves on to f-survey.

## Say it

- "capture this idea"
- "spec this concept out"

## When to use it

When you have an idea worth writing down but you're not ready to decide anything about it yet.

## Not for

Decision-complete work (f-blueprint), settling decisions (f-survey), a job's own plan (the foreman's PLAN.md), or single Logbook cards (f-card).

## It's working if

- It wrote exactly one file, `foreman/ideas/IDEA-YYYY-MM-DD_<short-slug>.md`, or placed it inside an existing idea directory and said so.
- The file opens with a title, a date, a status saying the discussion is open, a banner saying it is not a plan of record and not executable, and one line on where it came from.
- Settled points appear as `A0…` agreements and open questions as `Q0…`, with the options as they were discussed, not resolved.
- Nothing in it was invented: no locked decision tables, no ordered tasks, no answers to questions you never answered.
- `foreman/blueprints/README.md` has one new bullet for it in the **Ideas** section, naming what blocks promotion.
- The report gives the path, a one-line summary, the counts of agreements, open questions and rejected options, and the blocking questions.
- It opened no job, wrote no plan or code, and staged, committed and pushed nothing.

## Where it sits

The path an idea takes from a brainstorm to jobs, exactly as the skill draws it.

```
brainstorm → /f-sketch → more discussion → /f-survey → /f-blueprint → /f-plancheck
  → foreman/blueprints/ready/ (plan carries its `gate: plancheck` line) → /f-schedule → jobs
```

## Common questions

### Why does it keep my open questions instead of answering them?

Its rule is fidelity over closure. An idea file with honest open questions is complete; one with invented answers is treated as corrupt.

### What if we have actually settled everything?

It says so and points you to `/f-blueprint` instead, so a finished decision doesn't end up as a weaker thinking file.

### How does an idea become a job?

Once its open questions close, it goes through `/f-survey`, then `/f-blueprint`, `/f-plancheck` and `/f-schedule`. The idea file itself is never executed.

### We talked about two ideas. Can it capture both?

One spec per run. If several distinct concepts came up, it asks which one to capture.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/f-idea` still works.

## Connections

- Leads to: f-survey

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-status.md

# f-status

Tell you in plain words where things stand and what's next.

Command: `/f-status`

Stage: Kit · Catch-up
Source: `skills/f-status/SKILL.md`

## On site

Only when you ask. Different from the short status lines at the end of every reply. It only uses what's in the current session and runs no tools.

## Say it

- "catch me up"
- "where are we"
- "I'm lost"
- "refresh me"

## When to use it

When you want a plain summary of where things stand.

## Not for

The 5-line status block every reply ends with (templates/J-STATUS.md).

## It's working if

- It answers at once, without running any tool: no git, no file reads, no subagents.
- The reply uses up to five blocks in order (where we are, done this session, right now, next, watch out) and skips any that would be empty.
- It stays around 200 words or fewer.
- The body has no file paths, command names or commit hashes.
- "Right now" is a health line naming the scope checked: `Healthy`, `Blocked`, `Waiting` or `Unknown`.
- "Next" is one action and says who does it, or reads `nothing from you`, and the reply ends there.

## How to call it

The two forms it takes, shown exactly as the skill lists them.

```
/f-status              # refresh on the whole session
/f-status <topic>      # narrow to one thread
```

## Common questions

### Why won't it check the code or the repo?

It reads only what is already in the session, so it can answer instantly. If it reaches for a tool, the skill has failed.

### What if the session was compacted?

It works from the summary and says so in one clause. It never invents details to fill a gap.

### Can I narrow it to one thread?

Yes: `/f-status <topic>` refreshes you on that thread only.

### Is it the same as the status block at the end of every reply?

No. That 5-line block comes from `templates/J-STATUS.md`. This is a fuller catch-up you ask for when you step back or come back lost.

### Will it reopen decisions?

No. A choice you already made is stated as a fact, not an option, and a settled caveat isn't repeated.

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/f-survey.md

# f-survey

Turn a rough request into clear decisions, one round of questions at a time.

Command: `/f-survey` (old name `/f-groom`)

Stage: Plan · Before a job · step 1 of 11 in the order of works (Shape the idea)
Source: `skills/f-survey/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before a job, step 1: turning an idea into decisions. It settles each choice by checking the actual code, so the plan written next has no open questions.

## Say it

- "survey this"
- "groom this"
- "this is still vague"
- "tighten this before we build"
- "what am I missing"
- "survey this out loud"

## When to use it

When a request is still vague or has open choices, before anyone writes the plan.

## Not for

The site walk (the machine check at the start of a job, METHOD §2). Not for writing the plan (f-blueprint) or cutting it into tickets (f-schedule).

## It's working if

- Each round opens with the survey layout: your call, settled by the foreman, on site, next round.
- "Your call" holds at most three questions, each with the recommended option first and starred.
- Anything the code or the evidence can answer sits under "Settled by the foreman", with the evidence named, not as a question to you.
- No question in a round depends on another question still open in the same round.
- It stops asking once another answer would only tune implementation detail.
- It ends with one self-contained commission block: in scope, out of scope, acceptance criteria, decisions with their reasons, the likely lane and the exact next action (`/f-blueprint <topic>`, or park it).
- It created no job, plan, code or commit along the way.

## What a round looks like

Every round uses this layout, exactly as the skill prints it. The markers are the skill's own.

```
👷 SURVEY · <topic> · round <n> of <expected>

🚧 YOUR CALL (<count>)
 1. <the question, one line>
    ★ A  <option, one line>   ← recommended
      B  <option, one line>
      C  <option, one line>
    Why A: <one line>

✅ SETTLED BY THE FOREMAN (no answer needed)
 · <a choice made on evidence, one line, with the evidence named>

📐 ON SITE (facts that shape the ticket)
 · <a measured fact, one line>

🔜 NEXT ROUND: <what comes after the owner answers, one line>
```

## Common questions

### Will it decide things for me?

It settles what the code and the evidence can answer, and says what it found. It asks you only the questions whose answers change the architecture, the scope or the acceptance. It hands a fork to a council only when you authorise it to settle questions on its own.

### Can I run it out loud?

Yes: `/f-survey --voice` runs it as a spoken conversation, one short turn at a time. It needs the voice add-on (`/speak`, an OpenRouter key and `npx tsx`). Without them, survey in text.

### Why did it stop before asking anything?

Its first step checks the end-game lock. If the last job's close-out isn't finished, it stops and names the missing steps, so new work never starts on top of an unfinished one.

### Can I survey while a job is running?

No. If a job is active it declines: questions about that job belong to its own scoping.

### What happens in an autonomous run?

There is no one to ask, so it answers each question itself with its recommended option, marks each answer as decided under the autonomous run in the ticket, and goes on. It stops instead when a question has no clear recommendation, or when an answer would take the job beyond its board entry.

### How is it different from the site walk?

The site walk is the check at the start of a job. The survey comes before any job exists, and settles what the work should be.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-sketch
- Leads to: f-blueprint
- Uses: model-council, agent-council, speak


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/model-council.md

# model-council

Ask a panel of AI models, each answering on its own, to help settle a design choice.

Command: `/model-council`

Stage: Plan · Settling a fork
Source: `skills/model-council/SKILL.md`

## On site

Before a job, when you allow it: f-survey can ask it to settle a design choice that doesn't need the code. The panel only sees a written brief, never the code. It needs an OpenRouter key.

## When to use it

When a design choice is stuck between options and you've agreed to let AI models weigh in.

## Not for

Panels that must inspect the codebase (agent-council). Not for what tests or an evaluation should decide.

## It's working if

- Before any spending, it frames one neutral brief: a single decision question, two to four options, the constraints, and a request to choose and name the strongest argument against the choice. Its own lean is not in it.
- It opens a one-shot picker for every run, where you choose 2 to 5 panel seats from different vendors and one auditor. It does not run without your pick.
- The host's own model family never sits on the panel or as auditor, and when a Player is declared, that vendor's seat is dropped and the reduced count is stated.
- Every seat gets the same scrubbed brief and sees nothing from the other seats, the chair or the repository in the first round.
- The result is a decision the chair owns, with every first-round position, the convergence, the surviving dissent, and the auditor's verdict with the chair's answers.
- It does not hand the decision back to you as a question, unless it needs an authority it does not hold, such as spending, publishing or deleting.

## Common questions

### When should I use it instead of agent-council?

When a written brief can carry the decision. The panel never sees the code. If the models need to inspect or test the repository, use `/agent-council`.

### Is it a vote?

No. It resolves arguments, not votes: agreement counts only when it comes with shared reasoning, and a principled dissent ships unchanged.

### What does it need to run?

An `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in the repo-root `.env`, and at least two working panel seats. With fewer than two, it stops and reports that no council was formed.

### Does anything private leave my machine?

The agent is told to keep the outbound prompts clean: no methodology bodies, user identities, private data, credentials or repository details, and to scan every payload for known confidential names before each send.

### When shouldn't I use it?

For empirical thresholds, tuning, or anything a test or an evaluation can decide. Those go to the evaluation.

## Connections

- Used by: f-survey


---

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/orca-pi-connect.md

# orca-pi-connect

Link the foreman to a Pi builder in the Orca pane beside it, and know when it finishes.

Command: `/orca-pi-connect` (old name `/pi`)

Stage: Run a job · Starting and running a job
Source: `skills/orca-pi-connect/SKILL.md`

## On site

Handing work to the builder in Orca: the foreman sends each work order itself and is woken up when the builder finishes. Comes with Pi's finish signal, starts Pi inside the job's folder without the trust question, and binds a pane it opened itself without asking.

## Say it

- "connect to pi"
- "set up the builder pane"

## When to use it

When the builder runs in an Orca pane next to the foreman.

## It's working if

- The builder pane is split to the right of the foreman, in the same tab, and started in the job's worktree with an assigned session ID.
- It puts the pane handle and session ID to you and waits for an explicit yes before sending anything.
- Round 1 gets back the job worktree's absolute path and READY, with the Stop log growing by at least one line for that session.
- Round 2 runs three separate `echo` commands, prints the matching `ORCA_TERMINAL_HANDLE`, replies `DONE`, and the Stop log grows by exactly one line.
- The session file for that ID exists on disk, written during the handshake.
- The report says whether the link is proven, with the handle, the session ID, both rounds, the log counts and the model in the footer.
- During a job it sends only a one-line pointer to each work order, and checks the disk before reading the builder's report.

## The five proofs

The five things the link must prove before any work is sent, exactly as the skill lists them.

```
1 binding   the foreman opened the pane itself (exactly one new pane, on its right, fresh SID, or the old SID in a §1b resume), or the owner confirmed the handle + SID
2 pane      Orca can target that binding and submit prompts
3 hook      Pi's global agent_settled extension logs ONCE per genuine turn end
4 replies   Pi answers, runs tools, and the reply is readable
5 session   the on-disk session file records the turn under the bound id
```

## Common questions

### Why not just watch for the pane to go quiet?

A long tool call looks the same as a finished turn. The Stop log is the only completion signal it trusts.

### Why does it assign the session ID instead of asking Pi?

Asking Pi for its own ID is not proof of identity. The ID is chosen when Pi starts, or worked out from the session files and a fresh Stop-log line.

### Will it approve Pi's prompts for me?

No. A trust or tool-approval prompt is surfaced to you, never approved with keystrokes. Starting Pi with `--approve` in the job's own worktree is the one deliberate, up-front trust.

### Where are the stop extension and watcher?

In this skill's own folder: `pi-extension/foreman-stop.ts` and `stop-watch.mjs`. Copy `foreman-stop.ts` to `~/.pi/agent/extensions/` on a new machine and restart Pi.

### What if the split reports an error?

An error or timeout from the split means unknown, not failed: the pane often opened anyway. It counts the panes in the foreman's tab again over about 10 seconds. If there is still no new pane, it stops and asks you to look at the tab, and splits again, with a fresh session ID, only after you say there is no new pane. It never opens the builder in another tab.

### Does the link make any decisions?

No. It only carries pointers. Merges, pushes and deletions stay with you.

### It used to be called something else?

Yes: `/pi` still works.

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/pack-review.md

# pack-review

Bundle the goal, the rules and the changes into one brief for an outside reviewer.

Command: `/pack-review`

Stage: Inspect · The end game · step 7 of 11 in the order of works (Inspect)
Source: `skills/pack-review/SKILL.md`

## On site

Near the end, the second review: the foreman writes one brief for an outside reviewer once the first review's fixes are in, and checks it before it goes out (templates/PACK-REVIEW.md). It removes anything that names a model or an AI company, so the reviewer judges the work, not who wrote it.

## When to use it

Once the first review's fixes are in, to prepare the brief for the outside reviewer.

## Not for

Not a planning or build pack, and not a review (f-inspect, xreview).

## It's working if

- The output is one fenced block you can copy as it stands, with no commentary before or after it.
- The brief has its sections in order: goal, hard constraints, non-goals, what to review, the diff or artifact, tests or repro, and what not to relitigate.
- Nothing in the brief names a model or vendor: commit trailers and vendor-identifying paths are replaced, not summarised around.
- Paths are absolute wherever the reviewer may run in a different checkout.
- On a huge diff, it packs the file list and the riskiest hunks, and says what it left out.
- It did not review the work, rewrite it, or edit any file.

## Common questions

### Does it review the work?

No. It only builds the brief. The review happens in another session with `/xreview`, and the result comes back here for `/adjudicate`.

### How does the brief reach the reviewer?

Either you copy the block and paste it into the other session by hand, or an unattended run passes it to `scripts/cross-review-dispatch.mjs`, which seats a reviewer from another model family and runs it headless.

### Why strip model and vendor names?

The reviewer must not learn which model did the work, so it judges the claims, not the author.

### Can the same session review its own brief?

No. Running `/xreview` on work this same session produced is never valid. Independence comes from a different session, or a different process on another vendor's CLI.

### Where does it fit in a job?

In the end game: the foreman runs it for the independent inspection, after the lens inspection's fixes, and checks the brief before it goes out.

## Connections

- Comes after: f-inspect
- Leads to: xreview

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/speak.md

# speak

Read one reply out loud as a short spoken summary.

Command: `/speak`

Stage: Kit · Voice
Source: `skills/speak/SKILL.md`

## On site

Any time: the voice add-on. It can also read f-survey rounds aloud. Needs scripts/speak.ts, an OpenRouter key and Node.

## Say it

- "say that out loud"
- "read that back"
- "explain that aloud"

## When to use it

When you'd rather hear a reply than read it.

## It's working if

- You hear a short plain-language explainer, not the reply read out word for word.
- The spoken version has no code, file paths, headings or bullet points, and runs about 20 to 60 seconds.
- The rewritten text is saved to `scratch/speak-input.txt` and played with `npx tsx scripts/speak.ts scratch/speak-input.txt`.
- The chat reply is only a speaker symbol, plus a one-line note if the script printed an error.
- It speaks that one reply only, and later replies stay silent.

## How to call it

The two forms it takes, shown exactly as the skill lists them.

```
/speak            # explain my previous message aloud
/speak <text>     # explain/voice the given text instead
```

## Common questions

### What does it read out?

Your previous assistant reply, or the text you pass after `/speak`. It rewrites it as a short spoken explainer rather than reading it verbatim.

### What do I need to set it up?

Node with `npx tsx`, the bundled `scripts/speak.ts` and `scripts/bootstrap-env.ts`, Windows audio playback, and the repo's `.env`. The default engine is Grok Voice through OpenRouter, so it needs `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

### Can I change the voice?

Yes. Set `SPEAK_GROK_VOICE` to `eve`, `ara`, `rex`, `sal` or `leo` (the default). Setting `SPEAK_PROVIDER=hume` uses a saved Hume voice from `SPEAK_VOICE_ID` instead.

### Does it fall back to another engine if one fails?

No. It uses only the engine named in `.env`.

### How do I keep it on for every reply?

Use `/converse`. `/speak` is one reply at a time.

### Can I see the text it spoke?

Not by default. Ask and it will show it.

## Connections

- Used by: converse, f-survey

Source: https://toppingout.dev/skills/xreview.md

# xreview

Review another session's work with fresh eyes: list each claim, never rewrite it.

Command: `/xreview`

Stage: Inspect · The end game · step 7 of 11 in the order of works (Inspect)
Source: `skills/xreview/SKILL.md`

## On site

The second review: run in a new session from a different AI company (codex when the foreman is Claude), by hand or with scripts/cross-review-dispatch.mjs. It starts by confirming it hasn't seen the work before, and it never counts on work the same session wrote.

## When to use it

When the brief is ready and a session from a different AI company can review the work.

## Not for

Ordinary in-session code review (f-inspect, lens-code) and not for work this session wrote.

## It's working if

- It opens with an Independence statement: automated dispatch or hand-carried, and if hand-carried, whether it already knows the author or has seen the work.
- It states the goal it reviewed against and says whether that goal was stated or inferred.
- Every finding is a numbered row in the claim table (C1, C2 and so on), with a bucket, a severity, evidence and the smallest suggested change.
- Anything it could not check is marked UNKNOWN, not promoted to a defect.
- A clean review is a single `C0 | No findings` row naming what it actually read.
- It ends after the six sections, with no essay, no rewrite and no file edits.
- It refuses, and says why, when asked to review work this same session wrote or supervised.

## Common questions

### Who should run it?

A fresh session of a different model family from the one that did the work. You can paste a `/pack-review` brief into it by hand, or `scripts/cross-review-dispatch.mjs` can run it headless.

### Will it guess who wrote the work?

No. It is told never to guess the author, vendor or model, and not to mention model names even if the artifact leaks one.

### What does it judge against?

Only the stated goal and constraints in the brief. Items on the non-goals or do-not-relitigate lists are settled: it files no claims against them, and if one looks unsafe it says so once under Unknowns.

### What if the brief has no goal?

It asks one short question first. If you tell it to go ahead, it infers the goal in one sentence and labels it as inferred.

### Does it comment on style?

Only when style causes a real defect. It doesn't praise by default or invent nits to look useful.

### What happens to its output?

It goes back to the session that did the work, where `/adjudicate` judges each claim.

## Connections

- Comes after: pack-review
- Leads to: adjudicate
